entities.summary:
Peter the Iberian was a Georgian royal prince, theologian, and philosopher who played a pivotal role in shaping early Christianity and Christian Neoplatonism. As a prominent figure of the 5th century CE, he is often credited with founding the school of thought that would later be associated with Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite.

Born in the kingdom of Iberia, modern-day Georgia, Peter's rise to prominence was likely influenced by his connections to the Christian Church and the Byzantine Empire. His teachings, which emphasized the importance of spiritual contemplation and the nature of God, resonated with a broad audience and helped establish Christian Neoplatonism as a dominant force in early Christian thought.

Peter's legacy extends beyond his own writings, as his ideas influenced a range of subsequent thinkers, from Gregory Nazianzus to John Scotus Eriugena. His impact can also be seen in the development of Eastern Orthodox theology and the continued relevance of Neoplatonist thought in contemporary philosophical debates.

In conclusion, Peter the Iberian's significance lies not only in his own contributions to early Christian theology but also in the lasting impact he had on the intellectual landscape of Europe and beyond.

and literary figures of 5th-century Christianity. Sent as a political hostage to the court of the Eastern Roman Emperor Theodosius II in Constantinople as a child (c. 423 CE), he was raised in the imperial court alongside the emperor's sister Pulcheria and received a classical Greek and Christian education. Around 423 CE he escaped or was released from the imperial court, converted to ascetic Christianity, and became a monk — spending the rest of his extraordinarily mobile life as a wandering ascetic-scholar across the Byzantine and Eastern Mediterranean world: Palestine, Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor, and his homeland Georgia (Iberia).

Peter the Iberian is significant for two major reasons: first, his life is a primary source for the complex Miaphysite (non-Chalcedonian) theological controversy that dominated 5th-century Christianity. He was a committed opponent of the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE) — which defined Christ as having two natures in one person — supporting instead the Miaphysite position that Christ had one united nature. His connections to Miaphysite theologians and his influence on the theological debates of the eastern Mediterranean make him an important figure in the history of the Chalcedonian schism that ultimately divided Byzantine Christianity from the Egyptian Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian, and Syriac Orthodox churches.

Second, Peter the Iberian has been proposed by modern scholars (most notably Cornelia Horn and Robert Phenix) as the actual author — or one of the key figures associated with — the Corpus Dionysiacum: the influential body of mystical theological writings attributed to 'Dionysius the Areopagite' (supposedly a disciple of Saint Paul, 1st century CE) but actually composed in the late 5th–early 6th century.
